body:
What Is Electroplating?

Many metal objects have a shiny appearance or resist corrosion because their surfaces are covered with a thin layer of another metal.

Examples include chromium-plated bicycle handlebars, decorative metal fittings and jewellery coated with gold or silver.

Electroplating is the process of depositing a layer of a desired metal on another material by using electrical energy.

The coating may improve appearance, reduce corrosion, increase resistance to surface wear or provide another useful surface property.

Basic Principle of Electroplating

Consider a common arrangement for depositing copper on a conducting object.

  1. The object to receive the coating is connected to the negative terminal of the external electrical supply. It acts as the cathode.
  2. The object is placed in an electrolyte containing dissolved copper ions, such as a suitable copper sulphate solution.
  3. When electrical current passes through the system, copper ions gain electrons at the cathode and are deposited as metallic copper on the object's surface.
  4. In an arrangement using a copper anode, copper from the positive electrode dissolves and helps replenish copper ions in the solution.

The deposited coating is therefore created through an electrically driven chemical process.

The specific electrode materials and electrolyte depend on the metal being deposited. A dissolving metal anode is common in some systems, but it is not a universal requirement of every electroplating process.

Uses of Electroplating

Chromium Plating

Chromium provides a bright metallic finish and useful resistance to corrosion and surface wear. It is used as a surface coating on products such as bicycle handlebars, vehicle parts and bathroom fittings.

Making an entire object from an expensive coating metal may be unnecessary. A less expensive base material can provide strength, while the coating provides the desired surface characteristics.

Gold and Silver Plating

Jewellery and decorative articles may be coated with a thin layer of gold or silver. This gives them the appearance and some surface characteristics of the coating metal without requiring the whole article to be made from that metal.

Tin Coating

Tin-coated steel is widely associated with food containers. Tin provides a relatively corrosion-resistant surface that helps separate the contents from the underlying steel.

A damaged tin coating can expose the underlying iron or steel, so the effectiveness of the protective layer depends on its condition.

Zinc Coating

Zinc coatings protect iron and steel against rusting. Zinc is more reactive than iron and can provide protective action even where limited parts of the underlying steel become exposed, provided sufficient electrically connected zinc remains.

Zinc coating is often described as galvanisation. However, galvanisation does not always require electroplating; zinc can also be applied by methods such as hot-dip galvanising.

Electrolytic Refining of Metals

Electrolysis is also used to purify certain metals. This process is called electrolytic refining.

Copper is a familiar example. Copper obtained from extraction processes may contain impurities that are undesirable for applications requiring high electrical conductivity.

Basic Arrangement for Copper Refining

  • Positive anode: Impure copper.
  • Negative cathode: A thin sheet of pure copper.
  • Electrolyte: A suitable solution containing copper ions, commonly acidified copper sulphate solution.

When current passes, copper from the impure anode dissolves into the electrolyte. Copper ions are deposited as copper metal on the pure cathode.

Some impurities remain dissolved in the electrolyte, while certain insoluble impurities collect below the anode. The deposited material is called anode mud.

Electroplating and Refining Are Different

Both processes use electrical current and metal deposition at the cathode, but their purposes are different.

  • Electroplating: Deposits a chosen metal coating on another object to improve its surface.
  • Electrolytic refining: Produces more purified metal from an impure source of that metal.

For example, copper plating may place copper on an iron object, whereas copper refining deposits purified copper obtained from an impure copper anode.

Electrolytic Extraction of Reactive Metals

Electrolysis is also used in obtaining highly reactive metals from suitable molten compounds. Metals such as sodium, magnesium and calcium can be obtained through electrolytic processes involving their molten salts.

These metals are too reactive to be obtained economically from their compounds by some of the ordinary chemical reduction methods used for less reactive metals. Aluminium is also produced industrially by an electrolytic reduction process.

Thus, electroplating, electrolytic refining and electrolytic extraction represent different industrial applications of the chemical effects of electric current.

Prelims focus

  • Electroplating deposits a desired metal coating using electricity.
  • The object receiving an electroplated metal coating acts as the cathode.
  • In common copper electroplating, copper is deposited from copper ions at the negative electrode.
  • In electrolytic copper refining, impure copper is the anode and pure copper is deposited at the cathode.
  • Anode mud contains certain insoluble impurities from electrolytic refining.
  • Trap: Electroplating improves a surface; electrolytic refining improves metal purity.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 14, Chemical Effects of Electric Current, Section 14.3, Electroplating, printed pp. 178–180, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, Sections 3.4.5–3.4.6, printed pp. 52–53, consulted textbook edition.]

body:
Electrolysis in Chemical Manufacturing

Electrolysis is not limited to depositing metals. It also produces important industrial chemicals by using electrical energy to bring about chemical reactions.

One major example is the chlor-alkali process, which uses an aqueous solution of sodium chloride as its principal salt feedstock.

The Chlor-Alkali Process

An aqueous solution of common salt, sodium chloride, is called brine.

When brine undergoes electrolysis in a suitable industrial system, 3 important products are obtained:

  • Chlorine gas: Produced at the positive anode.
  • Hydrogen gas: Produced at the negative cathode.
  • Sodium hydroxide: Obtained in aqueous solution.

The name chlor-alkali comes from chlor, referring to chlorine, and alkali, referring to sodium hydroxide.

Uses of the Products

ProductWhere obtainedImportant uses
ChlorinePositive anodeWater treatment and manufacture of chemicals including PVC-related products
HydrogenNegative cathodeFuel applications and manufacture of ammonia
Sodium hydroxideIn the aqueous product streamSoap, detergents, paper and other chemical industries

These products are chemically different even though they arise from the same overall industrial process.

Electrolysis of brine must not be confused with electrolysis of suitably prepared water. Both can produce hydrogen at the cathode, but brine electrolysis produces chlorine at the anode under the conditions used in the chlor-alkali process.

Producing Hydrogen from Water

Electrical energy can also split water into hydrogen and oxygen. This is a different application of electrolysis.

Hydrogen produced using electricity generated from renewable sources such as solar or wind power is commonly described as green hydrogen, subject to the applicable emissions standard.

The process uses an electrolyser, which supplies electrical energy to the water-splitting reaction. Hydrogen is produced at the cathode, while oxygen is produced at the anode under the appropriate operating conditions.

Hydrogen can then serve as a fuel or industrial feedstock. Its important potential applications include fertiliser production, petroleum refining and certain industrial processes.

Why Electricity Source Matters

Electrolysis consumes electricity. Hydrogen produced by electrolysis is therefore not automatically free from greenhouse-gas emissions.

If fossil-fuel-based electricity supplies the electrolyser, emissions may occur during electricity generation. Using renewable electricity can substantially reduce the emissions associated with hydrogen production.

The hydrogen acts as an energy carrier: electrical energy is used to produce it, and the hydrogen can subsequently be stored, transported or used in another process.

This should be distinguished from a rechargeable battery, which stores energy through chemical changes within an electrochemical cell. Both involve chemical energy, but their storage arrangements and applications differ.

Prelims focus

  • Brine is an aqueous solution of sodium chloride.
  • The chlor-alkali process produces chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide.
  • Chlorine forms at the anode and hydrogen at the cathode during chlor-alkali electrolysis.
  • Water electrolysis produces hydrogen and oxygen under suitable conditions.
  • An electrolyser uses electrical energy to drive a chemical reaction.
  • Trap: Hydrogen produced using any electricity source is not automatically green hydrogen.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 2, Acids, Bases and Salts, Section 2.4.3, Chemicals from Common Salt, p. 30, 2026–27 reprint; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, National Green Hydrogen Mission, January 2023, Section 4, Sourcing Green Hydrogen; Press Information Bureau, Green Hydrogen: Emerging Pillar of India's Clean Energy Transition, 28 October 2026, sections on hydrogen production and electrolysers; sources consulted 3 November 2026.]

body:
What Is Corrosion?

Metals are widely used in buildings, bridges, vehicles, electrical equipment and machinery. However, many metals undergo chemical changes when exposed to substances present in their surroundings.

These reactions can gradually damage the metal or change its surface properties.

Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of a material, particularly a metal, due to chemical or electrochemical reactions with its environment.

Corrosion may occur through reactions involving oxygen, water, acids or other substances. The appearance and rate of corrosion depend on the metal and its surroundings.

The rusting of iron is one of the most familiar examples of corrosion.

Rusting of Iron

Iron exposed to moist air gradually develops a reddish-brown coating called rust.

Rust consists mainly of hydrated iron oxides and related compounds formed through the reaction of iron with oxygen and water.

Rust differs from the original iron in its chemical composition and physical properties. Its formation is therefore a chemical change, not merely a physical change.

Conditions Necessary for Rusting

Under ordinary atmospheric conditions, both oxygen and water are required for iron to rust.

  • Iron exposed to moist air: Rusting can occur because both oxygen and moisture are available.
  • Iron exposed to dry air: Rusting is greatly inhibited because moisture is absent.
  • Iron exposed to water without an available oxygen supply: Ordinary rust formation is greatly inhibited because oxygen is unavailable.

The presence of oxygen alone or water alone is not sufficient for the familiar rusting process under ordinary conditions.

Why Moisture and Salt Accelerate Rusting

Rusting involves electrochemical changes at the iron surface. When water is present, it can provide a medium through which ions move, allowing the corrosion process to proceed.

Increasing humidity generally increases the opportunity for rusting because more moisture becomes available.

Dissolved salts can increase the electrical conductivity of surface moisture and often accelerate corrosion. This is one reason iron and steel structures exposed to saline coastal environments may require additional protection.

In Gujarat, coastal infrastructure, port equipment, vehicles and outdoor steel structures can be exposed to humidity and salt-containing air. Their corrosion risk depends on the specific exposure conditions and the effectiveness of protective measures.

Corrosion of Other Metals

Corrosion is not restricted to iron. Different metals produce different surface compounds.

MetalCommon visible changeMain surface product
IronReddish-brown rustHydrated iron oxides
CopperGreenish coating after prolonged atmospheric exposureOften basic copper carbonate
SilverBlack tarnishSilver sulphide formed by reaction with sulphur-containing substances
AluminiumThin surface oxide layerAluminium oxide

The surface changes are not equally harmful in every case. Rust on iron is generally porous and does not provide a reliable long-term barrier against further attack.

In contrast, the thin oxide layer that develops naturally on aluminium is generally protective because it adheres to the metal surface and slows further oxidation.

Corrosion Is Broader Than Rusting

All rusting is corrosion, but not all corrosion is rusting.

Rusting specifically refers to the characteristic corrosion of iron or iron-containing materials. Copper develops a greenish patina, and silver may become black through tarnishing. These changes are examples of corrosion, but they should not ordinarily be called rusting.

Why Corrosion Matters

Corrosion can weaken structural components, damage metal surfaces, reduce the useful life of equipment and increase maintenance costs.

For example, uncontrolled corrosion of a steel bridge component may reduce its effective cross-section and strength over time. The visible condition of the surface alone does not always reveal the full extent of deterioration.

Protecting metals from corrosion is therefore important for safety, economic efficiency and the durability of infrastructure.

Prelims focus

  • Rusting is a chemical change involving iron.
  • Ordinary rusting requires both oxygen and water.
  • Humidity and dissolved salts generally accelerate rusting.
  • Iron develops reddish-brown rust; copper may develop a green coating; silver may acquire black tarnish.
  • Aluminium naturally forms a thin protective aluminium oxide layer.
  • Trap: Corrosion is the broader phenomenon; rusting is its familiar iron-related example.

[NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 6, Physical and Chemical Changes, Section 6.3, Rusting of Iron, printed pp. 63–64, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 4, Materials: Metals and Non-Metals, Section 4.2, printed pp. 46–47, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, Section 3.5, Corrosion, printed pp. 53–54, consulted textbook edition.]
